227.t: Production numbers for You're Never Too Young
227.s: Mandel did big dance numbers and Basie-like writing for a marching band in a Martin and Lewis film, thanks to Lou Brown, but does not count it as his first film.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Oh, I’d just do production numbers, those kind of things, the big dance numbers, ‘cause I’d learned how to do that stuff when I was doing the Show of Shows.

227.t: Percussion chase cue and the problem of telegraphing
227.s: Mandel describes the seven-minute percussion chase cue and his dislike of music that telegraphs what will happen on screen.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Oh yeah, that was a chase, that was when they were arresting her… when they finally caught up with her. I thought it was about a seven minute cue and I thought it worked very nicely because it provided the momentum that we needed for that whole thing, to get you through that chase. You know the…

227.t: Spotting, the music editor and computing the cue
227.s: Mandel describes spotting sessions, working from the music editor's timed breakdown, plotting a climax backward from its hit point and conducting to picture.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: pretty much before, then I have something to talk to the director about. So, that's how I like to proceed, then when we start talking the general procedure is we decide where music should begin, where it should end, which is a process called spotting, we spot where music will be in the film. Then…

227.t: Orchestration help under deadlines
227.s: Mandel explains that television deadlines force composers to bring in help for the mechanical work, and Kirchner notes Bill Holman orchestrated from his detailed sketches.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Oh, sometimes they give you impossible – you know, first of all movies used to have better more leisurely schedules especially if there was a decent budget on the picture but television ruined that. Now they give you impossibly close deadlines, so very often you need people to come in and receive…

227.t: Scoring The Americanization of Emily and The Sandpiper
227.s: Mandel describes his first big MGM string section on Emily and the jazz-flavored Sandpiper score for Big Sur exteriors, with Jack Sheldon's trumpet.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: Okay, well, “Emily,” was the first song, we’ll get back to that when get on songwriting. Then I got The Sandpiper, after that. I was starting to say about Emily getting back to that, that was the first time I had like a really good fat string section from MGM, the MGM staff string section and a…

227.t: Radio Tokyo speakers and the Japanese jazz records in MASH
227.s: Mandel recalls the awful 1949 Japanese jazz records that inspired the Radio Tokyo loudspeaker device, Altman's announcements, and cutting footage to music.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: and somehow I remembered that. And when I started seeing – you remember those things we did like the Pidgin, “My Blue Heaven,” and things like that. Well the early Japanese jazz records were just dreadful, they played them instead of [sings standard boogie-woogie] boogie-woogie was in 6/8 [sings…

227.t: Watching the film first
227.s: Mandel describes how he likes to watch a rough cut alone before discussing the score with the producer and director.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Well generally speaking, let’s say that there is no prerecording, you don’t have to record any music say before the picture is shot, and you only have to do that in case something is visually sung or danced, or played on the screen, you have to record the music first before it’s shot. Let’s assume…

227.t: Backing into film scoring
227.s: Mandel says Jack Lewis got him the job, that he did not push for film work, and that doors only opened again in the early 1960s after B pictures.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: I wasn't, I wasn’t, I did everything else in this business first, before I did movies and I just kind of backed into them rather than was out there rushing for them and I was, you know, I was happy doing what I was doing.

227.t: Hummers and writing his own orchestrations
227.s: Mandel defines Hummers, composers who cannot write music and hire orchestrators, and says he orchestrates everything himself because he hears it all in his head.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Oh God, there’s so many of them around Hollywood. Those are the guys who really can't even write down music but they get hired to do scores, and they’ll hum some, like a little fragment of a theme to an orchestrator who’ll take down the fragment of a theme and they’ll say, “give me five minutes of…

227.t: The Russians Are Coming and the frightened chorus
227.s: Mandel describes scoring Norman Jewison's film with Hal Ashby editing and using nervous UCLA students to imitate a Red Army chorus.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: Oh, Harper, I did after, The Russians are Coming. Russians are Coming was a very nice experience, that was with Norman Jewison, and Hal Ashby was the editor and Hal and I had been friends for many years before that so it was just a nice experience. Good actors, it was a good movie, very good movie…

227.t: Motivic development and the twelve-tone Point Blank score
227.s: Mandel explains that he wrote Point Blank (1967) around a tone row and motif, as one of his favorite film projects.
227.ch: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
227.q: Sure, I’ve done that, Point Blank’s a good example of something I did in, fact I wrote that whole – That’s totally a twelve tone score, I wrote it around a row and a motif, a tone-row and a motif.

227.t: Mancini, Hefti and J.J. Johnson's Across 110th Street
227.s: They discuss composers' use of orchestrators, and Kirchner notes J.J. Johnson's percussion cue echoed Mandel's I Want to Live! cue.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: I can only speak to myself, Mancini always used an orchestrator but if you looked at his sketches everything was there. I don’t think Neal did a great deal of film. J.J. I don’t know what kind of film J. did, he’s a wonderful writer though and Neal is too.

227.t: Instrumentation of the I Want to Live! score
227.s: Mandel says he chose his jazz orchestra with four French horns and unusual winds because they matched the sounds in his head, creating the first all-jazz film score.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: They made the sounds that I heard in my head in conjunction with this picture. So, I never ever decide on a bunch of instruments ahead of time and then try to write music to fit it, instead I try to make the noises I hear in my head. When I say noises you know, music and…

227.t: Not writing dark music
227.s: Mandel says he does not naturally write dark music and has stopped writing background music for violent scenes, and that he once disliked minor keys.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: I don't by nature write dark music, I tend to like happy music and/or soulful music, but I don’t really like – that’s another reason I don't particularly like movies and doing movies and I won't do background anymore cause I don't want to write – I don’t like violence, I’m very, very opposed to it…

227.t: Jazz and Mulligan in I Want to Live!
227.s: Mandel explains the film's source music versus score, and that Gerry Mulligan appeared because the real Barbara Graham loved his music.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Well it wasn't really, yeah there was – I must clarify that though there were not two separate scores. One album was composed of source music which is music you know that’s not part of background music, it was actually used coming out of records or radios or whatever it might have been, like the…

227.t: Films after the Oscar: Pretty Poison and others
227.s: Mandel lists lesser pictures such as That Cold Day in the Park and Pretty Poison before MASH, noting the Oscar did not help his career.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: Well, some things, my memory is starting to fail me around then. I did… I’d have to go look at credits and things to remember.

227.t: Hollywood's reaction and Mancini's Peter Gunn
227.s: Mandel was passed over for an Oscar nomination because the old guard disliked jazz, while Mancini's Peter Gunn the same year helped crack the ice.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Sure didn't, got frozen right out, Hollywood did not take very kindly to jazz in those days. The old guard especially Dmitri Tiomkin and those people did not like something like this come along.

227.t: Why Mandel disliked television writing
227.s: Mandel considers television inferior to film and the graveyard of composers like Duane Tatro and Earle Hagen, and they chat about Hagen's Harlem Nocturne.
227.ch: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
227.q: Only as much as I had to, I never liked writing television. I always considered it a far inferior medium to film, budget wise, schedule wise, quality wise, in every way. It was anytime you did TV it was like doing “B” pictures. In fact it took the place of, B, pictures, that’s what happened to, “B”…

227.t: Henry Mancini and the limits of jazz scores
227.s: Mandel calls Mancini the ideal film and pops composer, and says jazz or rock scores each fit only a small fraction of movies.
227.ch: Late career, producing and songwriting
227.q: Well, it’s growing and I’m happy to hear you say that. Hank Mancini is – left very big shoes to fill though, I’ll tell you that. He was my ideal of what the perfect composer was for films for pops, for almost anything. He was so elegant in everything he did; he did it right and on top of it he was…

227.t: Agatha, Deathtrap and other films of the 1970s and 80s
227.s: Mandel recalls Summer Wishes, Winter Dreams, Agatha and Close Enough for Love, Staying Alive, Deathtrap with two harpsichords, and The Verdict.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: Let’s see, I did before that I probably did, Summer Wishes, Winter Dreams, which was Death of a Snow Queen in its original form with Joanne Woodward. Got a nice little song out of that, they wrote with Alan and Marilyn Bergman called, “Summer Wishes, Winter Dreams,” fittingly enough. In fact they…

227.t: Winning the Oscar and its aftermath
227.s: Mandel describes Academy Award campaigning, winning in 1965, and the odd fact that the work dried up afterward.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: No. It wasn’t that it wasn’t a surprise it was just by the time the Academy campaigns and everything heated up, you know winning an Academy Award is pretty much like running for office, to be perfectly honest. That doesn’t mean to imply that there’s anything fixed about the voting, there isn’t, but…

230.t: Band shorts for Will Cowan and Snader Telescriptions
230.s: They sort out the film shorts he made for Cowan at Universal and for Snader, shown originally in bar machines, and the union's confusion over them.
230.ch: New Orleans, Havana and back to New York
230.q: Well, they must have made some kind of a deal with Universal. But I remember I made one for him, or maybe two, I don't know. But we didn't do them at Universal. We did them at some other studio, and I remember the musicians' union was there, they couldn't figure out what was going on and they were…

230.t: The Big Beat (1957) and using Barnet's band for the whole picture
230.s: Barnet accompanied the Mills Brothers in The Big Beat and Will Cowan then used his band for the rest of the film.
230.q: Well, no, like we -- the Mills Brothers and I did -- we accompanied the Mills Brothers. They worked it into the plot. And there was a little conversation, very little. We did a number and then we did a number with the Mills Brothers, and then that was it. And then Freddie Martin came in the studio,…

230.s: Will Cowan insisted on Skyliner in every short, including Bright and Breezy.
230.q: it from he, and he just loves that tune. And he'd insist, and I'd say, "Will, not again. Can't we do something else?" He'd say, "No, I want it in there."

230.t: Other film shorts: Movietone, Universal, Columbia and Snader
230.s: Barnet identifies shorts from 1947-51, recognizing Neal Hefti, Bud Shank and the California band in a still, and what company made each.
230.q: No. There's a blond young lady in front of the band there. This -- Harry Babasin on bass. It's very difficult to tell. This looks like -- let me get just a little more light on the subject here, and we'll see what we've got here.

230.t: Feather on Jazz compilations and Freddy Steps Out
230.s: Barnet says Universal let Leonard Feather re-edit shorts, and agrees Freddy Steps Out was a weak musical.
230.q: It seems to me that Will Cowan told me that Universal made a deal with Leonard to take a bunch of these shorts and re-arrange them or something and put them out.

230.t: Jasper in a Jam puppet cartoon
230.s: The band recorded Pompton Turnpike and Cherokee for a George Pal cartoon, with animation made afterwards.
230.q: Yeah, I remember that. That was a cartoon, you know, and we weren't seen of course in the whole thing. It's all cartoons.

230.t: Make Believe Ballroom and Melody Parade
230.s: They sort out the 1949 Make Believe Ballroom film, Martin Block versus Al Jarvis, and the Universal featurette Melody Parade with the Pied Pipers.
230.q: I would be inclined to think that Martin Block had arrested the supremacy of the battle of the Make Believe Ballrooms by then. I think more people associated -- around the country associated Martin with that than Al.

230.t: Record Shop, Redskin Rhumba and Sally, Irene and Mary: his brief acting career
230.s: Barnet says his acting was only sideline bandleading, and that sideline musicians rank lowest with directors.
230.q: Well, hardly. There's nothing lower on the totem pole with a director than a sideline musician.

230.t: A Song Is Born: everyone in Hollywood on the set
230.s: Barnet recalls the 1948 film with Goodman, Armstrong, Tommy Dorsey and others, shot while each led a band nightly, stretching a two-week job to seven weeks.
230.q: You know, that was quite a scene there. I was working at the Aragon Ballroom, and Tommy was working at the Casino Gardens, and Louis Lee Armstrong was working out at the Trianon, and Benny wasn't working anyplace, he got his sleep every night. But we'd crawl in and get a couple hours sleep, you…

230.t: Jam Session film (1944) and its recording personnel
230.s: They go through the film's cast and the personnel for Barnet's Cherokee, noting that Killian, McGhee, Holland and Pettiford were replaced on camera.
230.q: Yes. I had -- that's an interesting story, when we get around to it. I had both of them.

230.t: Idea Girl and the former band singer Laura Dean
230.s: The leading lady of Idea Girl had sung with Barnet at the Glen Island Casino as Laura Dean and ignored him on set.
230.q: I don't know. In our relationship there wasn't, you know, any trouble or anything. But she -- where she had been a very friendly girl, she was decidedly unfriendly. Could be that she didn't want anybody to know that she'd been a band singer, although I don't know what that would have to do with it.

230.t: Music in Manhattan: the studio orchestra instead of his band
230.s: For this 1944 film he recorded with Mischa Bakaleinikoff's studio orchestra because he had no band at the time.
230.q: Well, it wasn't my orchestra. It was the studio orchestra, because I had been having my jousts with the -- I went through induction seven times, you know, and everytime you figure, well, of course, this is it. And I was never in 4-F, and either they changed the laws or one time the guy decided I…

230.t: Back to California in 1932: sideline movie work and the Long Beach earthquake
230.s: He did on-screen band-directing in films such as Love and Hisses and Sally, Irene and Mary, and left before the earthquake; Willard shows him a book listing his film appearances.
230.ch: New Orleans, Havana and back to New York
230.q: I got my situation straightened away and I went back to New York and let's see, oh, somewhere in there I had been to California again. You say Cuba, see, we got all the way up to Cuba, which is '35, I was back in California in '32.

230.t: Syncopation (1942): the New York jam session sequence
230.s: The jam session with Krupa, Venuti and others was filmed in New York, and Barnet doubts Rex Stewart was in that segment because of Hollywood prejudice.
230.q: Well, the basic group that you mentioned, we did the recording of that in New York. The picture was actually made in California, but the jam session sequence, which I presume is what this is all about, with Gene and all the people you mentioned there, we did that over at 20th Century Studios on…

230.t: Studios refused to photograph Killian and Peanuts Holland
230.s: In Freddy Steps Out and Idea Girl studios used white stand-ins for Black sidemen Al Killian and Peanuts Holland, though their playing was recorded.
230.q: They put a ringer in for the actual picture. They made the recording, but -- well, this also was true at Universal there, that one picture there, the tune called, "Xango," X-a-n-g-o, was definitely Al Killian's trumpet that's featured all the way through it, and they wouldn't photograph him.

230.t: Charles Skinner and why the film was embarrassing
230.s: Barnet thought the producer insane when he proposed it, funded by ITT money; he found the finished film embarrassing for its montage of a girl dancing around New York, but likes the soundtrack.
230.q: Well, he -- I did a short for him somewhere, and he came in Basin Street when we were making this thing -- when we were playing there -- and I thought he'd flipped his cookies, you know. He said, "I'm going to do this," and I was staying across the street at the Waldorf and he was calling there,…

382.t: Offers and the move towards Hollywood in 1938

382.q: Well, I think we sort of anticipated a little bit there, because it takes time for a record -- from the time you cut it until the time that it's released --

382.s: She describes the picture, the cast, Matty Malneck's band, and being discovered washing clothes outside her cabin.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: when the picture was released, on the stage, with the picture. By this time, the record was out and everything was great.

382.t: December 1938 Victor session with songs from her films
382.s: Titles of the session, with 'Kind of Lonesome' from the film and 'It Ain't Necessarily So'.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: Yes. 'Kind Of Lonesome' is from St. Louis Blues. I think I mentioned before that after they padded my part in the movie, Hoagy Carmichael wrote 'Kind Of Lonesome', and there was a scene that sort of linked some of the bigger scenes together in which I sang 'Kind Of Lonesome' with Nat King Cole…

382.t: 'Say It with a Kiss' cut from the movie
382.s: The ensemble number with Dick Powell and Louis Armstrong was cut and survives on an album of deleted songs.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: It contains a lot of things that were cut from the movies. And I was on a show with Joe Franklin a few years ago, and he had it and he played it.

382.t: Dating 'Going Places' and the outtake record from Joe Franklin
382.s: Searching books and David Chertok for facts on the movie dates and a record of cut songs like 'Say It with a Kiss'.
382.q: The latest information I just read is, that it was made in 1938, and that I went out to Hollywood to appear in a club, which is perhaps true. And maybe because I was confused about the 1939 date, because the picture was probably made in 1938, but not released until 1939. So that just about clears…

382.s: Her voice was heard in other movies and Soundies, including the Benny Carter short and Dorothy Dandridge's scenes.
382.q: Yeah, it must've been. Those selections were done for, what at that time, a box -- I don't even know what you call it -- in which you can insert a coin and see the picture and see the performance and hear the songs too.

382.t: Making the two movies and the five songs she sang
382.s: In both films she was just in the movie; the songs in 'St. Louis Blues' included 'Loch Lomond', and she did little else on set.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: Well, you see in both instances I was just in the movie. They call it 'spots'. And although I was on the set of Saint Louis Blues longer than I was at Warner Brothers because I think I probably only worked at Warner Brothers about two weeks. But Saint Louis Blues was one of those kinds of movies of…

382.t: The Soundies and a short with Benny Carter
382.s: She made two Soundies in the Bronx, including one of 'St. Louis Blues', and Meeker's book lists a Benny Carter short.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: the machine, you know? I don't even know what you call the machine. But there used to be a machine that showed a picture and had the music. And I forget what you call those machines now. Sort of like pay television, or maybe the video disks now. (Like the nickelodeon.) "SOUNDIES"

382.t: An error in a French jazz-in-film book
382.s: The caption wrongly places her in a film that doesn't exist; confusion with 'Swingin' the Dream'.
382.q: Swinging The Dream. And, of course, it starts out with Bill Robinson and Shirley Temple, and a lot of other things that happened.

382.t: How the film 'St. Louis Blues' was retitled and later aired
382.s: The film was later retitled, and a friend saw her on the late late show under her own name.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: So, we sort of got over that little problem easily enough. As I said before, that was a make-it-as-you-go picture, because they actually my part. They created a scene -- I guess it was a scene just to link other scenes together where I was sitting alone, and there was the Nat King Cole Group behind…

382.t: An old tape, the outtake album and a film clip of 'Mutiny in the Nursery'
382.s: An early-1930s tape is with Alan Eighler; Chertok has the film clip she would like to show.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: It's over at The House That Jazz Built somewhere. He also had a copy, he had a tape of the concert that I did at Lewiston Stadium, the George Gershwin Concert. I sang "Summertime" and "Nights Work If You Can Get It".

382.t: The 'Going Places' sequence with Louis Armstrong
382.s: She describes the six-minute musical sequence, the Dandridge Sisters and the group of musicians.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: Now there was a sequence in the movie, 'Going Places.' In fact, I'd been listeining to the Louie Armstrong Festival, and I was --

382.t: Her view of the Hollywood experience while opening a club
382.s: She wasn't happy making the picture but was a success at the club she opened in Hollywood; she was out there in 1939.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: I was working in a club at the same time. I was having tremendous success. I was out on the Strip. I was working at the Versailles, which later became Mocambo, or something like that.

382.s: A tape from a Chicago friend; the last session on which Claude worked with her, with Hollywood musicians.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: And, of course, some of these things I had lost years ago, and even lost track of -- forgot that I had made them. And it was very good to have them so I could recollect.

382.t: The Hollywood session songs and musicians
382.s: Songs like 'I Dream of Jeannie' and 'Corn Pickin'' made with California musicians including Red Callender and Eddie Beal.
382.ch: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
382.q: I'm happy about the whole thing. I don't know. Now it may or may not be significant. Maybe he was happy about the whole thing was over.

88.t: Stand-in band work on film sets and Earl Dancer
