88.q: Okay, let me tell you what that was, what they were doing then. You used to go to a lot of films, and you would see black musicians on the bandstand, but that was when you were working as extras, you know, you really don't play the instrument, you know, you're just part of the scenery, and if you…

88.t: Freelance film dates: Hazel Scott, Lena Horne and Minnelli
88.s: Lee cannot name many films, but remembers dates for I Dood It with Hazel Scott, Lena Horne pictures, and a Minnelli scene with trumpeter Jack Trainer.
88.q: Well, Vincente Minnelli -- I was trying to recall, but I'm sure it was Busby Berkeley that did "Strike Up the Band" -- but Vincente Minnelli, what I did with him was some of the things that I did with Lena Horne. There was one thing that we did out there, I don't know what it was -- I can't…

88.t: Drum parts and night shooting with Louis Armstrong on a Mae West picture
88.s: Lee wrote march-with-four-feel drum parts for a Mae West film shot at night, where Louis Armstrong told stories between takes.
88.q: Oh, another movie that I did at Paramount Studios with Louis Armstrong and Mae West. Now I don't know the name of that movie, but that was the one where I wrote the drum parts for it because they wanted it to be a march, but they wanted to have the feel of 4/4 type of thing. And I'll never forget…

88.t: Columbia Studios music department: Stoller and Bakaleinikoff
88.s: Lee describes Morris Stoll and Misha Bakaleinikoff at Columbia, and the practice of reusing music, which was banned in 1977.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: So Misha was at Columbia, but Misha was not the first man. Morris Stoller was the head of the music department and he was number one conductor there. He did all the biggies there.

88.t: Freelancing in the studios as the only black musician; Calvin Jackson
88.s: At MGM and Columbia Lee played for dancers like Astaire, was the only black musician in the studios, and recalls Calvin Jackson denied composer credit.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: and did a lot of things with Manny Klein. As a matter of fact, at the time, Manny Kline and Rafael Mendez were on the staff at MGM; they had staff musicians then, and Johnny Greene was there and George Estolle was there, and Lena Horne's -- which was not her husband at the time, but was to later…

88.t: Setting up the timpani; The Jolson Story and Rita Hayworth films
88.s: Lee worked out how to arrange five timpani for crossovers and played traps on musicals including The Jolson Story.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: Oh, the first day was something. It came off, but it was -- you know, there's a trick to everything. In motion pictures, and in music, too -- you have to find out this particular thing, it was a matter of how to set the timpanies, you know, and by me being there that early, this is not tuning and…

88.t: First studio job: coaching Billy Lee for The Coconut Grove
88.s: His first studio job was recording the drums and teaching the child actor Billy Lee to mime them at Paramount.
88.q: Oh, yes I did. I left a big space out there. I was wondering what I was doing in '38 and '39 -- now I remember other things I was doing. Okay, my first studio job, okay -- my very first studio job was ... gee, it was at the Paramount. Paramount Studios called me, they had a young boy named Billy…

88.t: First day on staff at Columbia: five timpani for an Ann Miller picture
88.s: His first Columbia picture required him to play melodic timpani parts, so he arrived early to study the music.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: And so we had one out there, anyway, so I was there, and I worked on -- the first picture, I remember very well, the first picture we did there was with Ann Miller. I was trying to think of the title of it, but my first day there, I have to play 5 timpanies. They had written a part that the timpany…

88.t: Ray Heindorf, Lunceford at Warners and bringing in black players
88.s: Lee freelanced all over town, praises Ray Heindorf's support for black bands, and brought Marshall Royal and others to the studios.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: Anyway, he had him to do something. And then I got to the place at MGM, and I was working there so much and they -- you know, I had made a pretty good reputation, and then they wanted -- they said they wanted a good trumpet player, a good saxophone player, a good trombone player, as they would say,…

88.t: Winning the Strike Up the Band job by teaching Mickey Rooney
88.s: Lee beat other drummers for the MGM job by showing Mickey Rooney how to play the time step and break on drums.
88.q: Raymond Scott Quintet! Yeah, the drummer was named Johnny Williams, and he was supposed to be top. So they sent to New York to get him to do this, you know,but the trick in it, you know, you had to teach Mickey to play, you know, and there was a great drummer ... well,

88.t: No other black musician on staff; Lionel Newman and Benny Carter
88.s: Lee says no other black musician joined the Columbia staff, and Benny Carter declined a Fox composer-arranger offer from Lionel Newman.
88.ch: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
88.q: Right. But anyway, I'm just saying, ever since I can remember, the closest anyone came to being on the staff was Lionel Newman was very fond of Benny Carter, you know -- very fond of Benny Carter. And when Benny Carter had his big band down here -- you know, Benny used to do a lot of work at 20th…

88.t: Mickey Rooney on drums, Jackie Cooper and MGM's big office
88.s: Willard and Lee discuss Rooney learning drums, Jackie Cooper being the actor who could play, and who agreed to Lee's terms.
88.q: The guy that could play of those movie actors was Jackie Cooper. He was the one that could play, because he used to always come in to clubs and we'd let him sit in. But the rest of them, they had to have somebody play for them.

88.t: Conductors he worked under and Phil Moore's Astaire film
88.s: Before Nat, Lee worked under the Bakaleinikoffs, Stoloff, Heindorf and others, and played drums for Phil Moore's score for Fred Astaire's One for My Baby.
88.q: And when I started conducting for Nat, it was really a simple thing, and the guys thought that I had been conducting for ages, but I had not. And then again, I had worked under so many good conductors, you know -- I worked under both Bachalegnakoffs, you know, I worked under Morris Stoloff, I…

88.t: Playing the soundstage solo from memory while sitting on the music
88.s: Lee recorded the featured drum part with a 45-piece orchestra and, to be noticed, sat on his music and played it from memory.
88.q: Oh yes. Yeah. I worked on the movie -- it seemed like for ages, because I started off -- when I started off working at MGM, I used to have to take the S car -- you know, the street car, and transfer to something else and they would put me off and then I would get the bus and then I would be in…

88.t: Hiding at Val Verde from the MGM music head
88.s: Lee and Jimmy Blanton hid in Val Verde while MGM sent a limousine to find him because only he could teach Mickey the solos.
88.q: So I left. Jimmy Blanton and I were very, very dear friends, and we went up to a place called Val Verdi, you know, and I told my mother that -- and my sister -- that if MGM tried to get me, don't tell them where I was, because I ...

380.s: He lists the musicians in the Gjon Mili film short.
380.ch: Tatum, Wiggins and Los Angeles friends
380.q: Well, in the early 1940's, maybe 1942 or 1944, I don't remember which, we did Jammin' the Blues. Gjon Mili produced this. This was another thing that Norman, I guess, was co-producer on. On this was Billie Holiday, John Simmons, Jo Jones, Sweets Edison, Lester Young, Marlowe Morris was the piano…

380.t: The film New Orleans with Louis Armstrong, 1947
380.s: Callender played bass with Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Bigard and Kid Ory in the film, and calls it a high point.
380.q: And jumping ahead to 1947 (which I seem to be good at jumping around) was another film that I enjoyed doing. This was with Louis Armstrong, also Billie Holiday, and Barney Bigard, Kid Ory, the guitar player Bud Scott,

380.t: A Frank De Vol picture call for MGM
380.s: He cannot recall the film title but remembers playing tuba in a brass band on "California, Here I Come".
380.q: Not really. All I remember is it's for MGM. It hasn't come out yet. It should be easy enough to find out the name. I'll let you know next time.

380.t: The MGM film I Dood It with Hazel Scott and Lee Young, 1943
380.s: Callender recalls a featured spot with Hazel Scott and Lee Young in the Red Skelton picture.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: Yeah, well, I worked in the movie studios way back in the early Forties. I was reading in one of your books here, I Dood It, that was in 1943, with Hazel Scott and Lee Young...

380.t: First film Think Fast Mr. Moto and "jazz" as a dirty word in pictures
380.s: They go through film credits in Meeker's book; Callender says he made money only after distancing himself from jazz, and contractors asked if jazz players could read.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: That was one with Nat Cole, where Nat played the part of W.C. Handy. I think Eartha Kitt was also in that picture -- although she's not a Jazz singer, but she was in the picture.

380.t: The New Orleans set photo and the other people in it
380.s: Callender identifies Mantan Moreland, Frenchy Landry and Susan Harbin in a photo from the 1947 film, and says Harbin is married to Calvin Bailey.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: Mmm-hmm, and who's married to the great artist Calvin Bailey, who is my... Calvin and I went to school together...

380.t: Playing background music for the film Gypsy
380.s: He recalls Rosalind Russell's 46 takes and playing with Shelly Manne.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: Oh, I played in the background music in that picture, with Rosalind Russell. The thing that stands out in my mind about that is that Rosalind Russell actually sang some of the songs. You know, she wasn't really a singer, and so we probably did about 46 takes on one thing that she did, and they…

380.s: Willard reads the cast list of the Handy biopic with Nat Cole and Callender names Nelson Riddle.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: And Nat Cole had the title role.

380.t: Playing in the desert for Blazing Saddles with Count Basie
380.s: Callender and Willard talk about the brief big band scene shot in the Mojave, with wind and sand, and the long waits on film sets.
380.q: because you know how the wind blows in the desert at times! The wind was so strong that day until it almost blew all of us off of the stand.

380.t: Sideline film work in the 1930s and 1940s
380.s: He recalls bit parts, being placed in the background because his red hair did not fit the typical role.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: Yeah, I did a lot of sideline in pictures. As a matter of fact, I just remembered one, some Jungle picture. Nat Cole and I were both in the picture, Lee Young also. The funny thing about pictures in those days, they'd call typical Black musicians or typical Black people, and sometimes I didn't fit…

380.t: The Buddy Holly Story shoot in Jackson, Mississippi, 1974
380.s: Fox hired him as an Apollo bandleader, the project was cancelled after three weeks, and he joined the Screen Actors Guild.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: But that soured me on Las Vegas. I've never felt the same about it. And that's one reason I've spent most of my career never going South, until 1974. Twentieth Century Fox called me out for an interview one day, and they wanted me to play the bandleader in a picture about Buddy

380.t: Jerry Fielding and his first steady TV show, The Life of Riley
380.s: He started studio work with Fielding's orchestra, first on the William Bendix show, scoring background music.
380.q: She wrote the lyric to that. Because during that same period is when I was working with the Jerry Fielding Orchestra, and getting my feet wet in the studios. My first steady show was The Life Of Riley.

380.t: Lawrence Welk and the "Primrose Lane" theme for The Smith Family
380.s: Callender defends Welk, and tells how his one pop hit became a TV theme and how its royalties helped after the Sylmar earthquake.
380.q: I was on that, too. No, Lawrence Welk I guess a lot of people don't understand. But what's wrong with Lawrence Welk? I like him. He plays the melody. And also, at least once or twice a year, he writes a tune I wrote, my only Pop hit tune, "Primrose Lane." So every time I would see him, he'd say,…

380.t: Hello, Dolly in Los Angeles and Mort Stephens's film call
380.s: Callender subbed on tuba for the Carol Channing Hello, Dolly and mentions a call for a new TV film.
380.q: Jim Self on tuba the other day. And speaking of studios, I guess everyone has heard of Mort Stephens. He's the guy who did the theme song for Hawaii Five-O and Police Woman and several other shows. Anyhow, business has been rather slow around town, I hear. And I got a call from Dateline(?) just…

380.t: Recording in every idiom: Sons of the Pioneers, Gunsmoke and Hawaii Five-O
380.s: He says he has recorded everything from symphonies to the Sons of the Pioneers and background music for television shows with no credit.
380.q: Yeah. I would say all idioms from symphony to Sons of the Pioneers -- I recorded with them many years ago. So I've run the gamut.

91.t: Learning film scoring while keeping the band
91.s: Interested in film scoring, he did arranging and orchestrating off and on but no composition until about 1958.
91.q: Yes, I became interested in, you know, in wanting to know more about film scoring, and more about composition, which I had not studied to that time. And ... but I worked with Alfred

91.t: Stanley Wilson and Universal after Alfred Newman
91.s: His association with Stanley Wilson began about 1958 through composer Herman Stein and an M Squad solo.
91.q: Well, I was doing a thing with a friend of mine, Herman Herbert Stein, who was a composer at Universal Studios. He and Mancini had worked together quite a lot. We were working on a film ... I think it was, oh, what was it -- it must have been an M Squad (PROTOTYPE); it was a segment of something,…

91.t: The Snows of Kilimanjaro and the blues with three titles
91.s: He appeared as saxophone soloist in the film, playing an Alfred Newman tune that had three titles.
91.q: Yes. Well, I appeared in the film as, you know, a saxophone soloist. I did some writing; I don't remember the extent of it now, but it was just some, you know, arranging. That was ... let's see, was that Hugo Friedhofer or was it Bernie Herman's picture.

91.t: Black composers in Hollywood and bringing Oliver Nelson out
91.s: Carter notes more black composers now work in Hollywood and recounts recommending Oliver Nelson for a Universal job.
91.q: Well, I guess notably, Quincy Jones; that's the first one the pops into my mind. First name. Gee, Quincy ... I don't know when he came; he did "The Pawnbroker" -- I don't know what year that was. But up to now, he's done over 30 films, you know.

91.t: Neal Hefti brought west for a picture
91.s: Neal Hefti was invited to Hollywood for his Basie sound, not at Carter's instigation.
91.q: That's one particular case, but of course I know that Neal Hefty was invited out there under somewhat similar circumstances, not by any instigation of mine, but I know Dick Klein was telling me that when, I believe it was "Sex and the Single Girl" ... he wanted that sound that Hefty had been…

91.t: Working with Alfred Newman on Stormy Weather
91.s: Carter arranged source music for singers like Lena Horne and admired music director Alfred Newman.
91.q: I thought so, yes. He was a very, very kind man -- a man for whom I had a great deal of respect and admiration. He was what I considered a super musician, and he had had a great deal of experience in the field of, you know, scoring for films.

91.t: Buck and the Preacher and scoring the Louis Armstrong TV film
91.s: He scored Buck and the Preacher (1972) and the 1975 Armstrong television film produced by Dick Berg.
91.q: Yes. But prior to that though, we did the picture, 'Buck and the Preacher', which I think was 1972, which starred Sidney Poitier and Harry Belafonte, which was a picture that I did all of the music for, you know, the original music to.

91.t: The Hanged Man and the "Only Trust Your Heart" title mix-up
91.s: He scored the TV film The Hanged Man; his song with Sammy Cahn lyrics was wrongly credited because of an identical title.
91.q: An interesting thing about that song, "Only Trust Your Heart" -- I don't know that I've told you about that before, but Sammy Cahn wrote the lyrics to that song.

91.s: Carter was musical director and arranger for the Sammy Davis Jr. film.
91.q: Sixty-five, sixty-six, yes. And I went to New York, spent, oh, four to six weeks probably, doing that.

91.t: Starting in television and recording with Stanley Wilson
91.s: Stanley Wilson asked him to score M Squad segments, his introduction to TV and to full composition and underscoring.
91.q: And Herman had done it as a composer and Stanley Wilson was the music head, and after we finished doing this, and I had met Stanley. he asked me if I'd be interested in doing composition on 'M Squad,' you know ... doing a segment.

91.t: Film credits: Five Pennies, American in Paris, Panic in the Streets and others
91.s: Carter lists his arranging and playing roles on several films.
91.q: And I played, you know, on the soundtrack on the background what Jimmy Dorsey was supposed to be playing in the picture.

91.t: First West Coast engagement and Stormy Weather
91.s: At Billy Berg's Swing Club in Hollywood his band stayed eight weeks, and Mike Gould offered him arranging work on Stormy Weather.
91.q: And that was on Las Palmas Avenue at Hollywood Boulevard. Actually, a little bit north of Hollywood Boulevard. Run by a man named Billy Berg. My manager at that time was Carlos Castell, who was also the manager of Stan Kenton, and I believe, Sonny Dunham's orchestra --and we went in to this club --…

91.t: Flower Drum Song and TV series work
91.s: Carter recounts arranging and orchestrating for Flower Drum Song and episodes of Bold Ones, Ironside, Night Gallery; TV and film mechanics are the same.
91.q: I didn't do a great deal. I did some arranging, some orchestrating, and I played in the orchestra.

91.t: Jim Patrick, Serpico and Great Gatsby offers declined
91.s: He turned down film calls for Serpico and The Great Gatsby to stay at Princeton.
91.q: Oh, I had a call from Sydney Lumet to work on a picture called 'Serpico' -- and I also had a call from Bill Stinson from Paramount in Hollywood to work on a picture called 'The Great Gatsby' -- and I, at the time, he wanted to know if I ... I think it was on a Wednesday, and he wanted to know if I…

91.t: No blacks in the studio orchestras
91.s: Carter kept his band for security because few blacks worked in film; only Lee Young held a studio contract.
91.q: I guess -- I guess that's the feeling, you know; you wonder how much time can you put into this and what can you look forward to, you know, and as long as I had the band, I sort of felt that I should hold on to that for a little security, although I wanted to write for pictures, and at that time,…

231.t: His role in Cabin in the Sky
231.s: He explains how he was cast as go-between for Rochester, Ethel Waters and Lena Horne, and tells the love-triangle plot.
231.q: : Yeah. Well, the way I got in that show, someone called me in the theater and figured I would be just the one that could become the go-between Rochester, Lena Horne and Ethel Waters. So there was a love scene that they put up so that Rochester would be the husband of Ethel Waters and Lena Horne…

231.t: Other films: Calling All Stars in Britain with the Nicholas Brothers
231.s: He cannot recall songs from early Pathe shorts or the story of the British film Calling All Stars, remembering only friendship with the Nicholas Brothers.
231.q: Yeah, I was over there, American entertainer over there with the Nicholas Brothers, that's why they used me, I guess and I was known, too, so that makes it a little different also.

231.t: A Song Is Born revisited: talent unused
231.s: On Tape 11 he repeats that they had more talent than anyone in the film but were picked for a small part with little singing.
231.q: I didn't choose that, they picked us out for the part. We didn't pick the part. They picked us out for the part and that's the only thing they could find.

231.t: A Song Is Born: window washers who scat and play boogie
231.s: He lists the cast and says Buck and Bubbles played window washers with scat and a boogie, with no singing or dancing.
231.q: I can't sing from "A Song is Born," there ain't no song. I just dances only and Buck played the piano. Benny Goodman and all the rest of the musicians played on the instruments, had a jam session with it.

231.t: Dissatisfied with how Varsity Show used them
231.s: Nazarro arranged it from New York; Bubbles thought they deserved better songs and scenes and did not ask for them.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: I wasn't satisfied because I thought he should have been with us, because I thought we should have had better than we did in the picture.

231.t: The Pathe films and their all-colored casts
231.s: The Pathe shorts had a colored cast; he recalls titles like Black Narcissus, In and Out and Honest Crooks.
231.q: remember the names of any of these films? Yeah. Name of the film "Black Narcissus," "In And Out," "Honest Crooks" and I think of the one with ostrich, had an ostrich in one, can't think of that. But the place where you get your (inaudible) they got them, you got your film, they got those things,…

231.t: Casa Manana and going to California for Cabin in the Sky
231.s: Bubbles says they played Billy Rose's Casa Manana six weeks before doing Cabin in the Sky in 1941.
231.q: Oh, I played Billy Rose's "Casa Mañana." We played "Casa Mañana" just before we went to do "Cabin in the Sky." And we had to do that at the MGM studio, I think it was.

231.t: Arriving for Varsity Show with nothing written
231.s: They had no material, would take only the picture job, and made up their scenes themselves.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: That's it. They had nothing and we didn't do nothing. I wouldn't take no other job but the picture job. That's what I came back from England for to do the picture job. Either that or nothing. So we got the job in the picture, so we did the picture. Picture is over now if there's a job, okay, we'll…

231.t: The Orpheum circuit and the Hugh Wiley shorts for Pathe
231.s: After touring the Orpheum circuit to California they auditioned for Pathe and made eight Hugh Wiley shorts, working long hours under a director they had recommended.
231.q: So we go on the Orpheum circuit on bills with Frances White and Walker -- Walker-- can't think of his first name. And there are quite a few acts on the bill. However, However, we played the Orpheum circuit to California, we got into California and we got an audition to do for the Pathe' Studio, we…

231.t: Back in America in December 1936 with no picture arranged
231.s: He refuses other bookings and waits for the promised picture, suspecting Nazarro had paid to get them in a film.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: : No. No. We come back and we arrive in America in December 1936. I shall never forget. So the next couple of days we contacted the office to find out what the name of the picture was and what studio it was that we were going to be in and so forth, and he said they had no picture -- no, he said at…

231.t: Buck's boogie and disliking their part
231.s: He praises Buck making classics swing and says producers just wanted names, so he disliked the entrance and role.
231.q: That's the same way with this "Aneetra" s(?) Boogie" on the piano Buck had played, sextet from "di Lammemoor." He played "William Tell," he'd play any kind of piece you'd think about on the piano and make it ragtime, swing -- you knew all the a, b, and these people, long-haired musicians and they…

231.t: Varsity Show: no script, a coal-shovel janitor bit
231.s: With no music written they learned On With the Dance and Love Is on the Air; the director cast them as janitors, with Bubbles dancing while firing a furnace and Buck at the piano.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: No, just said movie. Just said movies, that's all. Got a contract for you for the movies. That's all. That's enough. And I figured he had a show, a picture for us so that did it. But he didn't have none because we lay off about two months almost before we got an answer back because I think it was…

85.t: Writing for film: timing, catching action and directors
85.s: Carter says cues must fit exact timings; he found directors' direction helpful rather than constraining.
85.q: Well, that, of course, was a great part of the difference, the timing, the writing to a specific, oh, two and three-quarter seconds or one minute and forty-two seconds and a half or something like that, and the music had to be tailored, or the particular cue had to be tailored just to that length.…

85.t: Advice from film composers, teaching himself, and the broadening effect of film
85.s: He exchanged ideas with other film composers and says film work broadened him.
85.q: Oh yes, there certainly were. Probably a number of people, you know. We used to discuss this and that about music and about film tracks. I would ask advice of them. They would ask advice of me. Oh yes, there was sort of exchange of ideas, primarily.

85.s: There was little difference from film except deadlines, which he found stressful but motivating.
85.q: Practically none. I don’t see the difference. The only thing is that when you’re writing for television, you just don’t have the luxury of time that you might have if you’re writing for theatrical film, because usually television shows, you know, they’re ground out every week, and usually when the…

85.t: Films he was proud of and ideas for later
85.s: He says it was all a gig and keeps stray ideas on separate paper.
85.q: I don’t know. I wouldn’t say that. It was all a gig, and I was happy to be able to do it and happy if they were pleased with it. If they were pleased with it and I was displeased, I figure they had the bigger vote.

85.t: Ghost writing, orchestrating and film credits
85.s: Carter says he was never ghost-written for, though in film he mostly developed another composer's themes as orchestrator.
85.q: If you’ve written it and your name is not on the screen, that only means that your name is not on the screen. But if you’ve written it and somebody else says “composed by,” and it’s somebody else, then that’s ghost writing.

85.t: Whether he played C melody saxophone on The Snows of Kilimanjaro
85.s: Berger says he played C melody on the 1957 soundtrack; Carter does not remember it.
85.q: Yeah. No, I don’t remember playing C melody on that. I remember playing C melody on something, but . . .

85.t: How work was handed out in Hollywood
85.s: Carter disagrees that work isn't commensurate with talent among studio players, and mentions rejected film scores.
85.q: I would disagree. I would disagree with that, because I think the studio musicians in Hollywood have all been at the highest height or degree of talent or proficiency or whatever you’d call it. There were some that would certainly get more work than others, and there were certainly many who were…

85.t: Black composers in the Hollywood studios before him
85.s: Carter names Phil Moore, Will Vodery and Lee Young and disclaims being a barrier-breaker.
85.q: Well, there was Phil Moore, who was very busy in the studios. I don’t know exactly what he did. Prior to him, I understand there was an arranger named Will Votary [phonetic] that, you know, that it was a little before my time here. Then I don’t know that

85.t: Background music and reusing film melodies
85.s: Music should be felt and not heard; unlike Mancini he has no songs that came from film scores.
85.q: No, not really. In many cases, though, many composers have. I mean, think of all the good songs that [Henry] Mancini has done that came from film scores, and one notable song, along with others . . . what’s [unclear] name? David Racks’ [phonetic] Laura. There have been many of those. I don’t think…

85.t: Was he stereotyped as a jazz writer in the studios?
85.s: He says no more than a white jazz writer would be.
85.q: I don’t think any more so than it would have been with a white musician that wrote so-called jazz. No, I don’t think so. I’d rather not think that I was hired because I was black, you know, in any instance.

85.t: Getting into film work through Stormy Weather
85.s: Mike Gould recommended him to Irving Mills; the pay beat the band, and he disbanded in 1946.
85.q: Well, while I was in Hollywood, there was a friend of mine named Mike Gould, who had been a long-time friend, actually, and one of my closest friends. He was working for the music publisher, Irving Mills, and Irving Mills was, I believe, coproducer or in some important capacity on a film called…

225.s: Goldsmith invited him into the booth and Johnson admires his Planet of the Apes score.
225.q: Earle Hagen, for the most part. Jerry Goldsmith was very friendly. I would go to his sessions and he would say, " Come into the booth." The recording booth is, for the most part, a no man’s land or a no-no for outsiders or strangers. Jerry Goldsmith is one of the giants, as far as film composers. I…

225.t: Other black film composers; observing Quincy and Lalo's sessions
225.s: Baker asks about Benny Carter, Quincy and Oliver Nelson; Johnson played trombone on Quincy and Lalo's calls.
225.q: I don’t recall that Oliver ever had a chance to do a feature film. His forte was mostly television. He may have done one.

225.t: Deadline pressure and rejected scores: Alex North and 2001
225.s: Editing delays squeeze composers and Kubrick threw out North's score.
225.q: At first, yes. It was quite difficult to adapt to because of that element, the pressure of meeting a deadline. Film production companies are notorious for fussing with a film forever in the editing process while the composer is standing in the wings, waiting for them to release it so that he can…

225.t: Stravinsky's story: music first, film second
225.s: A story of Stravinsky refusing to write after the film was shot.
225.q: The story goes that Igor Stravinsky was approached to write a film score and had a meeting of minds with the power structure and the powers-to-be on the film project. They proceeded to tell Mr. Stravinsky, "Mr. Stravinsky, here’s how it works. We shoot the movie. We cast the movie. We go on…

225.t: Television versus film work and the clique of composers
225.s: TV assignments were easier; a few composers dominate film.
225.q: Yes, it was easier. Al Bart had an easier time of getting assignments for me for television than for feature films. If the truth be told, there are only a few feature film composers who do most of the films in Hollywood. It's a very self-contained little clique of composers. It's Goldsmith and…

225.t: Starting in film and TV scoring with Earle Hagen
225.s: Work on shows like Six Million Dollar Man and Mike Hammer, and Hagen's help.
225.q: Oh, yes – a whole new world, shall we say. At first, I just went around and observed on film recording sessions. It was quite fascinating to see film projected on a large screen, and to watch a conductor give a down beat and see the music matching the film. I got more and more interested in that,…

225.t: Carter's original music and the film As Thousands Cheer
225.s: The band played some Carter originals and appeared in a movie on the West Coast.
225.q: Some of Benny’s original music, yes. I wish I could think of some of the names. He wrote some beautiful original compositions, and I can't recall what they were at the moment. I think we’ll have to research that.

225.t: Racial barriers in Hollywood film composing
225.s: His agent Al Bart was told they did not want a black composer or a jazz one.
225.q: I was fortunate to have a good agent. To be a film composer in Hollywood, you must have an agent. There is no such thing as going it alone, without an agent. I went with Al Bart, who was one of the best in the business. The truth of the matter is that Al had a great deal of difficulty getting…

225.t: Quincy Jones, The Pawnbroker and deciding to go to Hollywood
225.s: Watching Quincy and Lalo Schifrin scoring films led him to leave for California in 1970.
225.q: for a number of years, and it was only amplified by this new discovery about synthesizers which blossomed into all kinds of wonderful and crazy things in the electronic world [and] finally led to MIDI, which I am involved in now. That was the origin of that whole syndrome. With Mark Brown I began…

105.t: Meeting Hale Smith and the Dean Martin film
105.s: He met Hale Smith through Jim Hall, Hale arranged for Gongs East and Eric Dolphy studied with him, and they later did films, including a shopping story from Mr. Rico.
105.ch: Bebop, band changes and the road
105.q: No. I met Hale here in New York come to think about it, and he and Jim Hall knew each other because they were both from Cleveland and he came to a rehearsal we had and we hooked up and, you know, stayed friends ever since. And Hale did some charts for me, you know, but Jim Hall was the reason I met…

105.t: Scoring Repulsion: Polanski's freedom and the piccolo cue
105.s: Hamilton praises Polanski as a hands-off director, explains that film music is knowing when not to score, recalls his Mr. Rico score being ruined, and describes the piccolo and rhythm cues in Repulsion.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: Man, let me tell you something about Roman. Man, Roman was perhaps the best director that I have ever worked with for the simple reason man, I had 25 music cues in that and we only had discretion about one, one, in which he says okay, we’ll do it your way. But he left me completely alone and that’s…

105.t: The Sweet Smell of Success and Marty Milner's fake guitar
105.s: The film crew followed his group for six months to check they were clean, and Hamilton recalls Marty Milner miming guitar while John Pisano's arms did the playing.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: On Sweet Smell of Success man, they had followed me -- what I’m saying, me and my group, they had followed us for six months all over the country just to see if we

105.t: Tarzan extras as a child, the Dandridge orchestra, and film business views
105.s: As an eight-year-old he worked as a Tarzan jungle extra, later played for Dorothy Dandridge's mother, and thinks movies are cutthroat and short of good scores.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: You know all the Tarzan movies; they used to pick up us kids in a truck, a flatbed truck. We met on the corner. I forget which corner it was, on the east side. It was about no more then five or six of us, right, and we met on the corner and they’d pick us up and they’d take us out to the lot. They…

105.t: Paramount Studios staff rehearsal drummer with Callender and Dudley Brooks
105.s: He, Red Callender and Dudley Brooks were the only three black musicians on a major studio payroll, keeping time for starlets such as Marilyn Monroe and Sheree North.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: And there were only three of us, myself, Red Callender, and Dudley Brooks who was the pianist. And we were the only three black musicians in the whole entire Hollywood studio scene at that time, and what we did, what I did and what we did, like a rehearsal piano player, I was the rehearsal drummer.

105.t: Meeting Roman Polanski through Jerry Schatzberg
105.s: Jerry Schatzberg, a photographer-turned-director Hamilton met at the Vanguard, introduced him to Polanski in London, who asked him to score Repulsion.
105.ch: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
105.q: I hooked up with Roman Polanski with -- Jerry Schatzberg introduced me to Roman. He and Roman were good friends and Jerry -- I don’t know whether you’re familiar with Jerry Schatzberg’s work. You ever seen Panic in Needle Park, Al Pacino’s first movie? That was Jerry Schatzberg.

105.s: Hamilton notes that Red Callender was already established, and that they later worked together on staff at Paramount Studios.
105.q: Yeah, I did. Red and I worked quite a bit together. As a matter of fact, Red Callender, and myself, and Dudley Brooks, piano player, we were on staff at Paramount Studios. This was later.

491.t: Writing music for the French film Des femmes disparaissent in Paris
491.s: The Messengers recorded after their club sets, with Golson writing themes night by night while watching the film on a Movieola, similar to Miles Davis's score.
491.ch: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers
491.q: Yeah. In English it was The Disappearing Women. That’s what it was. We were playing every night at the club. We finished [at] one o’clock – something like that – and we did the recording after we finished playing. So we recorded until the morning hours. Art contributed some things, but it was only…

491.t: From Brandt lessons and a German ski film to moving to Hollywood and TV scoring
491.s: Golson had a few private lessons with Brandt, scored a German film, then moved to Los Angeles at Quincy's urging and scored It Takes a Thief, Mission Impossible and M.A.S.H.
491.q: we joined his class. I think he was teaching at Bennett [Bennington] College up in Vermont then – a girls college. I think it was a girls college. He used to come home on the weekends, Saturday and Sunday. So we studied with him. I think we had just – only two sessions. Then it fell apart. It fell…

491.t: Scoring to picture: streamers, click tracks and conducting
491.s: He describes scoring to film punches with streamers rather than click tracks, and conducting his own scores after a single lesson from Brandt.
491.q: which is mechanical, and you don’t have much feeling, or you do it by simply watching a big clock they have for you, that goes around. You got the tempo, you’re watching the clock, and you’re waiting for that streamer. It can be a long streamer or a short streamer. You wait for that punch, which is…

491.t: Spielberg wants him for a speaking role in The Terminal
491.s: Golson was in Europe when Steven Spielberg's office asked him for a role with Tom Hanks, and he did a screen test and corrected the line.
491.q: No. I was in Europe. The office called me one day and said, “Steven Spielberg called today and wanted to know if you were interested in a speaking role with Tom Hanks?” I said, “Oh, don’t believe that. That’s nothing.” I said, “Woody Allen called a few times, and I went there first couple of times.…

491.t: Shooting in Montreal and the plot behind his Great Day in Harlem scene
491.s: Spielberg built a nightclub scene around the Great Day in Harlem photo, with Hanks' character seeking Golson's autograph; Spielberg knelt to chat with him at dinner.
491.q: “Why don’t you do it again and say it” – now I’m going to add – do it the way you – so I did it, and they sent it back to him. He said, “Perfect.” Then he said, “We’re going to record in Montreal.” I had already done something up in – I can’t ever think of the name of that town – Palmdale,…

491.t: Filming with Tom Hanks, Quincy Jones and Spielberg's nickname 'Tack'
491.s: Golson describes the scene with Hanks, Spielberg's old fandom, and how a nickname he shared with Quincy Jones made Spielberg and Quincy call him Tack.
491.q: “Tom, where’d you get that suit? I got to get one just like it” – so he comes up to me, and he’s speaking with this accent. After the scene, I said, “You sound just like Dracula.” He wanted my autograph. He was reticent to talk to me. The band started to vamp Killer Joe. I said, “I got to play now,…

491.t: Black composers in Hollywood film and television
491.s: Golson lists Benny Carter, Quincy Jones and Oliver Nelson and says success depended on skills like timing more than on race.
491.q: There were a few. Before I got out here, Benny Carter, he was writing, and Quincy Jones. He came in – Quincy was doing well. Then Oliver came. The three of them, and then, with their bidding, I came. Then there were four of us. Then Benny faded away, started doing something else. Then Quincy got…

4.t: The Lincoln Theater ad and Popkin Productions
4.s: Willard asks about an ad for the all-colored film Four Shall Die and the Popkin company.
4.ch: Central Avenue clubs, Nordskog, Sheffield and Music Town
4.q: Well, that was a...the starting. That was the starting. They uh...first they ran the Burbank Theater at Sixth and Main for awhile and then they made the Negro picture, and I think Herb Jeffries was in one of their pictures, if I'm not mistaken. I don't know way back there but anyway, they still…

4.t: First screenplays for a producer of shorts
4.s: A producer of adult films talked of shorts and Spikes wrote Harlemesque; the man disappeared after marrying.
4.ch: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names
4.q: Yeah. Well, up there, after...after...uh... There was a white fella come along, and he was in...uh, I think, pornography, and he come up there, and he was a producer and a cameraman and all like that, and he come up there, and we got to talking about shows, and I wrote two...three of them. I got…

4.t: Making the Vitaphone film for Warner Bros. in 1927
4.s: While at the Follies Theater, Byron Foy hired Spikes's band to make a Vitaphone short for Warner Bros., about 45 minutes with entertainers and dancers.
4.ch: The Vitaphone film and studio work
4.q: Byron Foy came in and hired us to make the picture. Of the Foy Brothers. And we went out and made the picture for Warner Bros., and I showed you the letter, and he recommended the band very highly for Victor Record Company. And this was made...this picture was made before Al Jolson.

4.t: The store as hiring hall, booking office and film extras source
4.s: Musicians and entertainers hung around the store; studios called for bands and Black extras, until a man upstairs took over the booking and moved to Central Casting.
4.ch: Later ventures, lodges and San Francisco recollections
4.q: Well, they...they...all of the musicians and entertainers used to kind of hang around out there, you know, and... because, you know, sometime we'd have a job...Well, we'd get calls for four or five bands in a night, and then we'd have to hustle up bands for the rest of the engagement. And then…

4.t: Writing film shorts for the would-be producer
4.s: Spikes wrote several short screenplays with shooting notes for a producer who never made them, planning even a life of Lionel Hampton.
4.ch: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names
4.q: Well, I...as I told you, this white fella come up there, and he started to hangin' 'round there because he'd been...his place had been closed, and he had no place to hang out or nothin', and he come down, and he used to hang around there, and...and he had a cameraman that he knew and everything,…

4.t: Tom White's letter to Central Casting for Spikes
4.s: Spikes shows a letter from Tom White of the Hollywood Recording Company recommending him to Central Casting; he declined the job.
4.ch: Later ventures, lodges and San Francisco recollections
4.q: Oh, I think it was...uh, between '25 and '30--somewhere in there.

4.t: The 1947 Cavalcade of Jazz program page on Spikes
4.s: Willard reads a profile claiming Spikes organized a band in 1921, sent for Lionel Hampton, and led the first Black band recorded for Warner Brothers' sound film.
4.ch: Publishing, Jelly Roll in Los Angeles and band lore
4.q: I told you that Leon Heflin...Heflin...uh, put that...

69.s: Willard reads the personnel of the 1938 Paramount short with Florence Mills and Bessie Dudley; Tizol doesn't recall it.
69.q: No, I don't believe I ever worked with Florence Mills.

69.s: Willard describes a jukebox short of Caravan with Tizol's solo; Rose thinks he may not have known it was filmed.
69.q: Yeah. He was in the band doing it, and probably didn't even know they were doing it.

69.t: Check and Double Check: dark makeup for Tizol and Bigard
69.s: They were made up darker for the film and gave them cold cream; Bing Crosby sang Three Little Words.
69.q: And they gave us the cold cream and so forth, when we got through, to go there and wash it off and take all that stuff off. Oh, it was awful.

69.t: Hawk Talks, The Mooch and Murder at the Vanities
69.s: Willard lists more films; Tizol remembers only playing Hawk Talks.
69.q: Yeah, we played it with Duke Ellington, yeah.

69.s: He doesn't recall Paris Blues but remembers Murray McEachern and extracting the parts recorded in California.
69.q: Murray McGrekin. Yeah, he played a solo on something in the studio. We were making the picture, yeah, and we were doing the recording on it.

69.s: Willard lists Solitude, Sophisticated Lady, VIP Boogie and Symphony in Black; he doesn't recall them or Fredi Washington dancing.
69.q: The only time I remember Freddie Washington was at the Apollo Theatre, when we were playing the Apollo Theatre, for a Cotton Club show. Freddie Washington was dancing for Henry Whetsol. "Hyparna."

69.t: Films with Duke and Harry James; Belle of the Nineties
69.s: He names Check and Double Check and the Mae West picture and some James films, remembering little.
69.q: Oh, with Harry James -- I did one with Harry James and I did one with Duke, naturally. The first one was with Duke with the Amos and Andy picture.

86.s: Edison and Berger debate the year of the Norman Granz film shot by Gjon Mili.
86.ch: Singers, records and Jammin' the Blues
86.q: ‘Cause he was in the army. He stayed in the army until….let’s see, the war started in ’41 didn’t it? This was done in 1940.

86.t: Making the film: replaying solos for the camera
86.s: They recorded the sound track one day and had to mime their solos the next.
86.ch: Singers, records and Jammin' the Blues
86.q: There wasn’t too much process, it was just get up there and play. And the hardest thing was, after we had made our solos, we had to duplicate the solos the next day, which was hard to remember what you played the next day.

86.t: The film's reputation, personnel and Barney Kessel's hands
86.s: He lists the players and they wonder why Kessel's face is never shown.
86.ch: Singers, records and Jammin' the Blues
86.q: No, in Europe, they charge to see it. We’re not getting any of the money, but they charge to see it. I know we got paid some money ‘cause Norman Granz wasn’t that type of guy. He always paid you more than what you would ask for. But that movie is a classic. I’ve seen it any number of times, it was…

86.t: Film portrayals of musicians: Ben Vereen, Teddy Buckner and Duke
86.s: Edison and Dance discuss who played Armstrong, why Teddy Buckner should have done it, and who might portray Ellington.
86.q: Cicely Tyson. She's -- oh, she's fantastic. She's a superb actress, you know. And Ben Vereen is all right, but he portrayed Louie Armstrong.

86.t: Movie soundtracks and how they pay
86.s: Edison played on film soundtracks such as Houseboat for Nelson Riddle and compares pay for movie and record dates.
86.q: Oh, yes. And Dave Klein he's the one that -- and I made the soundtrack for a lot of the movies, "Step Down to Terror" with Richard -- Anthony Quinn. And I made the soundtrack for "Houseboat" with Cary Grant and Sophia Loren. Jane Powell, the girl most likely -- Nelson Riddle scored all the music…

86.t: Teaming with Eddie Lockjaw Davis; Lady Sings the Blues
86.s: Edison tells how the Davis partnership began in 1977 after he did the trumpet work for Lady Sings the Blues and the Julie Andrews show.
86.q: We had been recording together in New York off and on. Riverside, we did an album, and we had known each other a long time. So we started corresponding about getting together, you know, and he was busy and I was busy, too, but I was doing good, you know, making records, and I had this -- I did 26…

239.t: Freddie Hubbard's cue and Marshall Royal's solo, with an Ellington lesson
239.s: Jones tells how he coached Hubbard to play what he saw on screen and treated Marshall Royal like a vocalist; Parks heard Ellington in it.
239.q: Well, this was a thing where I'd learned some things from Ellington, to put the human element in the -- into the person -- into the horn and to take the notes off the paper, because the notes cannot play. You have to have the interpretation, you know? And Freddie Hubbard was sitting Here's a great…

239.t: Playing stride piano behind Jimmy Rushing in The Learning Tree
239.s: A party performance led Gordon Parks to cast him as unseen piano player behind Rushing; the planned gag was cut.
239.q: Well, this is funny. This is at a party with John Levy and his wife, Gail Fisher at that time. And my wife and everybody, we were all just having a good time, so I sat down and started playing some tongue in cheek piano, stride, not realizing that it was going to become that important, and Gordon…

239.t: Scoring Shaft's Big Score with Gordon Parks and Tom McIntosh
239.s: He wrote five or six cues for the film, including Joe Williams's song, working with Tom McIntosh, Dick Hazard and Gordon Parks.
239.q: Yes, that's right. Because Tom was in the booth with Gordon at that time, you know, and discussing what this meant and what that meant and what this music meant to the picture. Because you know you have the very big screen there, and you have to explain to people the semantics, musically what it…

239.t: Telling Freddie Hubbard to play what he sees on the Shaft screen
239.s: A second telling of how Jones had Hubbard turn his swivel chair and play the bedroom scene.
239.q: And this was a funny scene where Shaft was in the bedroom with his lady. And I told him, I says -- he asked me, he said, "Jimmy, what do you want me to play on this?" I said, "Turn your chair around and look at the big screen and see what Shaft is doing and play that."

239.t: Peace Corps special, Perry Como and film work
239.s: Jones lists a Belafonte Peace Corps special, a Perry Como show with Ella and being called by Gordon Parks.
239.q: Belafonte. Now that's going back, oh -- Peace Corps thing. Sergeant Shriver was on it. I just had to write some scores, that's all.

239.t: Belafonte's show with Hank Jones on piano and Harry's free hand
239.s: Duke did not need to play because Hank Jones was on the track; Belafonte gave Jones latitude and he hired outside heavyweights.
239.q: And Duke didn't have to play, because there was Hank Jones in there playing. I had to put all that stuff together. But Harry gave me so much latitude. The only hard thing about it was just staying up around the clock. But all the other problems were out of the way. No political overtones or…

355.t: First TV composing job: The Bold Ones via Stanley Wilson, and Dave Grusin
355.s: Universal's Stanley Wilson hired him to score an episode of The Bold Ones; he also befriended Dave Grusin in the Howard Roberts Quintet.
355.q: Well roughly. I mean here’s what happened. The first, if I remember this correctly, the first job that I was offered to write an episode of a television show was Universal. The music supervisor at Universal was a guy named Stanley Wilson, a friend of my father’s, they had worked together, there are…

355.t: Scoring Dan August for Quinn Martin with Hollywood's best players
355.s: Grusin recommended him for Dan August; Scott conducted a top orchestra and recalls the elation.
355.q: Yeah, “The Fugitive,” “Cannon,” “Streets of San Francisco,” “Barnaby Jones,” and more. But this was a show in 1969 I believe starring a then-unknown actor named Burt Reynolds. And it was called “Dan August.” And Dave had written a great theme for this show, wonderful, wonderful theme. But he was…

355.t: Click tracks, frame counts and calculating chase cues
355.s: He explains click-track mathematics, the Carroll Knudson book and cue sheets for chase scenes.
355.q: That’s correct. It was, yeah, it was a whole separate science of how to make some hit, some chord or some thing in the music hit at exactly the right time where the gun is fired or the car takes off or there’s some bit of, you know, so there was a whole lot of

355.t: Hearing the score on the scoring stage and dictating changes
355.s: He discovers whether music works at the scoring stage and dictates fixes to the orchestra when producers ask.
355.q: Yeah. I’m trying to remember if I did. I’m sure I did I just don’t recall offhand, because of course when you look at a movie or score it from the cue sheets you kind of know it inside out so it’s always good to know whether your music works with the movie and of course you find that out on the…

355.t: Scoring to the finished picture and psychological scenes
355.s: He prefers to see a near-final film as a first audience member and enjoys scenes of psychological drama.
355.q: Right. Great question. Well obviously — needless to say — music for films and television is a highly subjective matter. And so the good news for me, for me as a composer, is I get to see the film for the first time when it’s basically complete except for the music. I cannot tell you how many times…

450.t: Auditioning for Throw Mama from the Train
450.s: After a recording break, she tells how Danny DeVito recognized her from Our Gang at her audition, and of the good food on set.
450.q: That’s very funny, talking about that, because a guy came into the club the other night, and he said, “I’m amazed. I didn’t know you sang.” I went to audition, which everyone has to do, in order to see if I fit the part of a principal of a school. No, no, no, no. That wasn’t it.

450.t: Yanks and driving a jeep for John Schlesinger
450.s: In Yanks with Vanessa Redgrave she plays a Red Cross woman and recalls the nervous jeep scene.
450.q: With Vanessa Redgrave. I don’t drive. I can drive, but not in traffic. So I only drive in movies and t.v. There was a scene where Vanessa and I are in a jeep. We have to go down this road, and we suddenly come across a huge area which is showers, and the guys are naked. Just before John…

450.t: Short Cuts and Wardell Gray's wife Jeri
450.s: She says she got Jeri a part in Short Cuts and recalls Jeri's humor and cooking.
450.q: I certainly knew what it was about. I got Wardell’s wife a little part. I told her to come on the set. I introduced her to Bob, and he gave her lines, which entitled her to become a member of whatever it is.

450.t: Leaving the trio; Robert Altman, The Player and Short Cuts
450.s: She explains she stopped at the group's height to sing alone, then describes how Kathryn and Robert Altman cast her in The Player and Short Cuts, and mentions Tardo Hammer.
450.ch: Altman films and the Metropolitan Room
450.q: memory. I know I’m right. Jon is a tremendous talent on his own. So I didn’t regret ever making the decision to stop. We stopped at our height. We were really getting to be more popular and more popular. But I just felt that if I stayed there, I didn’t want to hear what was being said, because I…

450.t: Working in television and film with Robert Altman
450.s: She says directors matter, and praises Altman for letting actors experiment and holding party-like screenings of dailies.
450.q: It depends on who your director is. Doing a t.v. show is an art in itself. Movies, it really depends on your director, I think. That’s why Bob Altman is so prominent in my life. He would let you experiment. He said to me the first day, “I want everybody to come to the dailies.” I, like a lot of…

369.t: Making Sensations of '45 and appearing with the picture in New York
369.s: In 1944 she played opposite Gene Rodgers in a circus scene with a deletable sequence and no lines, then did live shows with the film in New York; no other film followed.
369.q: I guess in the middle of the year. Me and my mother went to do “Sensations of ‘45” with Cab Calloway, Eleanor Powell, Woody Herman, and Dennis O’Keefe.

369.t: The MGM offer her manager turned down
369.s: MGM offered $750 a week for seven years but the agent took the United Artists deal at $3000 for one week; such film inserts could be cut for Southern audiences.
369.q: And that greedy agent, his name was Corkscrew Gervish, I called him. He took the deal from United Artists, $3000 a week and I only did a week. With MGM, I had $750 a week for seven years and he didn’t take it.

369.t: Crossing over to film and Broadway: only one of us at a time
369.s: In the 1940s you took whatever work the job called for; Nat Cole crossed over, but show business only made one Black star at a time.
369.q: You were anxious to just get work. You weren’t thinking about other venues, you were just thinking about getting work. You’re supposed to get work.

369.t: Staying with the Shacklefords and the cast of the Hollywood picture
369.s: She lodged in a private home in Hollywood and recalls the circus-like film with Cab, Eleanor Powell, Woody Herman, Sophie Tucker and Gene Rodgers.
369.q: It’s easy to get. Eleanor Powell, Cab, Woody Herman and Sophie Tucker. It was a circus. And Gene Rodgers and I played against each other. He was a very good pianist. Cab was directing and shaking his hair.

369.t: Leaving Chicago in 1944 for a Cab Calloway film and a crooked manager
369.s: She and her mother took the Super Chief to Hollywood for the Cab Calloway picture; the manager she calls Corkscrew Gervish took the $3000 deal instead of an MGM contract and skimmed commissions.
369.q: I left the Chicago area in 1944. I got a chance to do a picture with Cab Calloway called "Sensations of 45” and my mother went with me.

145.t: Sound-track calls from Forbstein and Georgie Stoll; first black contractor
145.s: Warner and MGM music directors called him after Sebastian's; Stoll made him a contractor for a Louis Armstrong street scene.
145.ch: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
145.q: Yeah, I started with the sound track playings. I used to get a whole lot of calls from out at Warner Brothers, First National, from Leo Forbstein (PHONETIC), who was the musical director out there. He used to come and hear me at Sebastian's Cotton Club and he cut a liking to me and thought I had a…

145.t: Contracting the Blazing Saddles desert scene
145.s: Royal also contracted musicians, hiring Red Callender, for the desert Basie scene.
145.ch: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
145.q: Yeah. I never saw it, but I heard it was a funny picture and I know a lot of people that have seen it three or four times. They thought it was so funny. But I always hire my old buddies, if I can, and Red was one of my old buddies. So I had Red on it, too.

145.t: Playing the feature tune in Shaft's second film
145.s: Gordon Parks insisted on Royal for a ballad in the second Shaft film, recorded in one rehearsal.
145.ch: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
145.q: I did some of the recording for the second Shaft. I did the feature tune of the thing. It's a ballad type thing and I played it.

145.t: Black musicians and the studios; Lee Young on staff
145.s: The best pay was in unseen recording; studios excluded black musicians except Lee Young at Columbia.
145.ch: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
145.q: I really couldn't tell you all the names of films. Many times, when you work in a film, the part where you make the most money is the part where you're never seen, which is the recording element of it. I guess during those days, during the early days of film recording, I was probably as much as any…

145.t: Film work: Westerns, Indian parts and being in-between
145.s: He worked on Westerns, played Indians and rode an elephant, owing to his light complexion.
145.ch: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
145.q: Well, I worked with all of the stars and things in those days. I worked with Hepburn, Richard Barthelmus, (PHONETIC), these are all people that you wouldn't really know about. Back with -- oh, gee. I never was much for names, but I worked with so many people. I just -- they all just run together in…

348.t: Scores thrown out: Earle Hagen and Barbra Streisand
348.s: Earle Hagen, composer of Harlem Nocturne, had an arrangement rejected by Streisand; other scores were dropped by producers.
348.q: Oh yes. There were lots of scores thrown out. One that I personally remember, Earle Hagen is a buddy of mine. He’s a great writer and he did —

348.t: Click tracks, streamers and Henry Mancini's scores
348.s: Playing to picture with earphones, click tracks and striping, and Mancini's jazz writing within click tracks.
348.q: We all had earphones, yeah, click track. One of the first people to do the click track thing and the — I forgot what they call it — they scratch the screen.

348.t: Clarinet on Northern Exposure with David Schwartz
348.s: He played clarinet for Schwartz's synth-based scores, the doctor character's instrument, and talks about composer cue royalties.
348.q: That was a lot of fun. David Schwartz, who was the writer, that was the first time I had — not the first time, I had been with some people who had used synths. Now David is a bass player and used synth for whatever sounds he wanted, and he used that as when he did his work he would work on the…

348.t: Coming to Los Angeles and the studio orchestras
348.s: His first trips west with Les, and the contracted studio orchestras at Fox, MGM and others.
348.q: Oh the very first time with Les was ’38. I mean just before I did those recordings with him back east, this was one of the stops we made. I guess we played the Palladium, stuff like that. So that was the earliest. Then we came out the second time, that was also a Palladium stop and that’s when they…

1012.t: Father's training and the range Hollywood demanded
1012.s: Early gig stories, then his father's path from streetcar driver to Marines, Washington University and a Ph.D. in composition, which let him write anything for Hollywood.
1012.q: Real early on in life. I’ve got a ton of stories to tell you about gigs and Dad and all that kind of stuff. And I’ve probably seen more than most because I’ve seen great players scuffle to play this music. You know but he just sets it down there and you’ve just got to count this stuff off and go,…

1012.t: Television work, Stanley Wilson and residuals
1012.s: Royalties from The Six Million Dollar Man, writing on the spot for Longstreet, mentor Stanley Wilson at Universal, other composers in Los Angeles, and Ironside.
1012.q: Well because they had to be prepared to do pretty much anything. It’s interesting you mention “The Six Million Dollar Man.” From a family royalty standpoint we still get paid for that stuff. Universal owns the rights to the music itself, but we get half of what they get, which is a really good…

1012.t: Moving to Hollywood and demand for African-American composers
1012.s: His father went to Hollywood, got an agent and a start at Universal, helped by 1960s demand for Black composers.
1012.q: Yeah, Dad was in New York for a while, but he always wanted to be a composer in Hollywood. That was something that he always wanted to do. The Marconis and the Newman Brothers and all those guys, Hollywood was where he really wanted to go. So he got an agent and he lived in the Beverly — oh what’s…

1012.t: The studio factory and the timing clock
1012.s: Coming home exhausted, and the clock and cue sheets used to time television cues to a tenth of a second.
1012.ch: Sound Pieces and Los Angeles studios
1012.q: That clock was the clock that he used to write music for Universal, for television. Because what they would do back then was they would give a cue sheet out and the cue sheet was all timed to a tenth of a second. So the Six Million Dollar Man throws this ball at 2 minutes 22 seconds, and the ball…

703.t: They Shoot Horses, Don't They? with Harold Land
703.s: They fronted the band in the film after Ray Brown was too busy.
703.ch: Harold Land and the West Coast return
703.q: Ray Brown – they had asked Ray Brown to do it. Ray was too busy. Ray was good friends with Harold. He said – Harold said, “Me and Bobby will do it – got a group.” He says, “What can Bobby do?” I grabbed a trumpet and acted like I was the leader of the band. So I became the leader of the band. So…

703.t: The Notorious Landlady, his first film, with Nina Simone
703.s: His first movie role came playing vibes behind Nina Simone in a scene with Jack Lemmon and Kim Novak.
703.q: No, not Sidney Pollack. But they suggested I – I think Sidney might have suggested it was okay, that I would be good in the movie, because Sidney was a director. Anyway, they asked that I go ahead, from doing They Shoot Horses, Don’t They? But that wasn’t the first movie I made. The first movie I…

703.t: Role in Round Midnight and the band with Billy Higgins
703.s: Dexter Gordon wanted him in the film; he became Ace and played with Billy, Herbie Hancock and Pierre Michelot.
703.q: That was – the Round Midnight movie, that was when they – when Bertrand Tavernier wanted to get Dexter to do this part, Dexter wanted me to be in it. That’s when I changed my name from – they wanted me to be called Red. I changed my name from Red to Ace. That was because of Ace Hutcherson, which…

703.t: Cooking in the Round Midnight apartment scene
703.s: He cooked real recipes from a friend on the set and fed the crew while Dexter shot other scenes.

One of the things are the performers, because sight reading, if they don't get the message right off the bat, forget it and they were good…

706.t: Working with Danny Kaye and Dick Powell on film sets
706.s: He recalls relaxed film work with Danny Kaye and Dick Powell's rehearsal style on Going Places.

706.q: So relax, you know? You didn't always stay to the script entirely all the time, did you? You didn't have to. I mean, how many times... Bing was... One time he was singing... 706.t: Childhood memories and the Paris Blues cast
706.s: He recalls selling newspapers and swimming as a child, then names Paul Newman, Sidney Poitier and Diahann Carroll as co-stars.
706.q: I mean, we sold newspapers to use the things, and we used to go swimming and play baseball. We used to think like kids did. How do you compare your life here in France with your life in the United States? Well, I was a little older here. I mean, I thought you were talking about when I was a child.

211.t: Learning film scoring and Victor Young facing Cecil B. DeMille
211.s: He learned scoring by watching; story of DeMille demanding melody from Victor Young's main title.
211.q: I think again by brute force. If you sit there — I sat in the orchestra and watched guys die in front of producers. Good composers. One: Aaron Copland — die in front of these, forgive me, idiot producers who want everything to sound like Wagner or something. I mean that’s the only name they knew…

211.t: Starting to conduct and the click track

211.q: Yeah, well I’ll tell you, you know how I started? The conductor wouldn’t show up. It was always in a panic. Often the conductor was the orchestrator or composer or arranger, dishwasher, and may times they’d be late on the date. So you know everybody’d be looking at their watch at whatever the call…

211.t: Dimitri Tiomkin and Bernstein's Philharmonic concerts

59.t: Film scoring for Woody Allen and other directors
59.s: Film scoring draws on everything he knows, requires working with directors and budgets, and cut music is a disappointment.
59.q: Well I found that film music writing demands just about everything I’ve ever known, not just one aspect or another aspect, but such a job requires just about everything I know, because I do my own orchestration. 59.t: Timing film cues and learning from 58-second commercials

59.q: Well it’s all different ways. If the background music is to be a specific song, why of course Woody and I will have talked about it beforehand and then it becomes a matter of arranging it according to what’s needed in the scene. If it’s original music I go to my piano and work out some ideas,…

991.t: How he scores films and how he got the Clint Eastwood job

991.s: He says directors typecast Latino composers as salsa-only, calls it a kind of discrimination, and describes few film opportunities in 14 years in Los Angeles.
991.q: I’m going to tell you, in general this is going to sound a little rough, but it’s what I really feel. If some people have some kind of stereotyped mentality in terms of jazz music and this and that, also in terms of to pick a composer for a movie, a lot of directors and producers have a stereotype…

991.t: Debbie Allen and 'Pepito's Story' for the Kennedy Center
991.s: He recalls working with Debbie Allen on a ballet and a musical, learning to write for dance.

618.s: Roger Kellaway conducted, Greg McRitchie orchestrated, and Dan Wallin's studio gave him a dream first film experience.
618.q: Well what I did is I was realistic. I amassed a wonderful team. 618.t: Getting the 'Invasion of the Body Snatchers' score
618.s: Philip Kaufman wanted him; he convinced producer Bob Solo and took a low offer that became well paid thanks to doubling.

618.t: Writing the symphonic and electronic score
618.s: He closed his office for five weeks, wrote for orchestra for the first time, and overdubbed Prophet synthesizer in exhausting work.
618.q: Tripling, quadrupling – with a fair amount of money. So the irony was I ended up being paid really quite well, and I had this unique experience of bringing to bear everything I had ever done in music, or wanted to do. Because I wanted someday to write for an orchestra and figured it’s never going…

588.t: Singers who all sound alike, and the film The Girl Can't Help It

588.t: Never wanting to be a star

704.s: Jones describes his first short film in Sweden, Sidney Lumet bringing him in on The Pawnbroker, the producer of Mirage being startled that he was black, Mancini's defense of him, and Cary Grant calling for his last movie.

704.s: Asked who helped him into Hollywood, Jones recalls skipping school for movies in Seattle, reading Earle Hagen's book, identifying Alfred Newman and Victor Young by ear, and later befriending the eastern European film composers.

102.t: Gordon Parks, Henry Brant and the call to score The Learning Tree
102.s: Parks's plan for a first Black film auteur led him to Henry Brant, who recommended Golson and McIntosh. Golson declined and McIntosh got the job.

102.q: There are two. I did The Learning Tree, which is the first. Then next one came. Gordon had an idea for a story—Shaft. He had heard Isaac Hayes had a demo and he loved his voice. In his demo, he had a new fangled discovery. Namely, that you could use your foot to push a pedal on the guitar.…

229.t: Silent movie work and Satchel McVea
229.s: He played atmosphere music on silent film sets, and Redd and Blakeney talk about Satchel McVea, who refused to join the union and found them work.

229.s: He recalls playing a cadenza in the RKO picture Cross Fire with Ory, Barney Bigard and others, a film about race.

229.q: The director told us to play at the opening and there was you know, they didn't use much music; didn't read much; no music involved, and so they had me play something like a cadenza to start off with; Barney Bigard was in that picture.

168.t: Appearing in Stormy Weather with Fats Waller
168.s: Stewart played in the Fats Waller sequence of Stormy Weather, his only time playing with Waller, whom he found comical and wonderful.
168.ch: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
168.q: Yeah, and -- Hell's A'Poppin' -- let's see. I was just wondering, I was thinking about another picture that Slim wasn't with me that I made with Fats Waller.

168.ch: Movies and the Los Angeles scene

168.t: Impressions of the movie business, Lena Horne and Bill Robinson
168.s: He was pleased to be in the film, paid about as for Hellzapoppin, and found Lena Horne and Bill Robinson down to earth.
168.ch: Movies and the Los Angeles scene

33.t: His brother Paul, drummer and sound-effects man in Hollywood

453.q: I believe "High Society" was on that. Because we had -- when we was said, ya ta ta, they had the spear shooting somebody, they had the spear going.

93.t: Freddie James' heel work and handstand split
93.s: Green compares Steele's heels to Freddie James, who did handstands onto his heels and a modern split, including a Step Brothers film scene.
93.ch: Split, hospital and decline of tap
93.q: Yeah, that's it. That's how you would come out of a hand stand. He did it in one of the east side -- I think it was the East Side Kids movie -- the Bowery Boys, something you know. With the Step Brothers -- that's what he done it with. He was a loader, you know. They had went to some stock room,…

566.t: 'Simply Heavenly' and her voice in movies and television
566.s: She played in a short-run stage show of Langston Hughes's 'Simply Heavenly', and her voice was used in films such as 'Panic in the Streets', 'My Blue Heaven' and 'The Steel Trap', though she never watched them. She did hear the television 'Come Home Bill Bailey'.
566.q: Yeah, some show in some theatre. I don't know. Out there on Santa Monica Blvd. or something.

29.t: Work in the Metro film studios
29.s: Howard says he played at Metro for a year, once on camera in 'Morosco's Penny Dance', never having mentioned it.
29.q: You couldn't get the years, stumbling around like I am. Ain't no way for you to get it.

94.t: The 1946 'New Orleans' film recording and Sidney Greenstreet's tails
94.s: Moore recalls the film session in Hollywood, the costume tails, and the brown shoes painted black.
94.q: Those records were the tunes out of the picture "New Orleans," you know what year that was made -- it was made in New Orleans. That was a wonderful experience, too, when we were in Hollywood in those studios. And one time one of the trumpet players who always loved brown shoes, so instead of…

384.t: Red Nichols's Five Pennies personnel and Manny Klein
384.s: He reads the personnel of a Five Pennies session; Kline notes Manny Klein dubbed taps in From Here to Eternity.
384.ch: Studio recordings of the late twenties and thirties
384.q: Leo Condilli, trumpet. Miff Moll, trombone; Dudley Fosdick, mellophone; Fud Livingston, clarinet; tenor; Art Miller, string bass. Chauncey Morehouse, drums, vibes, sometimes solo.

148.t: Dating his Paramount time against Boris Morros and the Raeburn records
148.s: They try to fix dates, Handy conducted the Jubilee date while Ike Carpenter played piano.
148.q: Right, it would have to be, it would have to be another pianist, because I conducted. I was standing in front of the band on that Jubilee date.

427.t: Honored in Kansas City: 'The Last of the Blue Devils' and Harry Truman
427.s: He made the Blue Devils film in Kansas City; asked about Truman, he says he was doing anything to make a dollar.
427.q: consecutive ring--loudly] is going to drown us out. There. Okay. You were the guest of honor up there, and then you answered questions. There was some reference to Harry Truman in Kansas City during that period of The Blue Devils.

30.t: Films in the discography: 'Bundle of Blues' and 'Belle of the Nineties'
30.s: Willard asks about early films; he does not recall 'Bundle of Blues' and identifies 'Belle of the Nineties' as Mae West's film.
30.q: Oh, that's when I was a youngster.

236.t: Los Angeles conductors and their downbeats
236.s: He rates conductors such as Billy May, Mancini, Rugolo and Newman.
236.q: But L.A. is a funny place. I don't know what it is. I like to live there. But the music, I don't like it. I like a lot of the conductors in Los Angeles. I think my favorite conductor in Los Angeles is Jack Elliott. I've played for under (you say you "play under," you know, when you play for a…

389.t: Why the Whiteman band looked like an advancement
389.s: The large Whiteman orchestra, with Grofe, Jimmy Dorsey, Chester Hazlett and a film planned, appealed to the young arranger.
389.q: I was elated and for an arranger, a guy who had just been arranging for a year, here was a band with strings yet. Four, only four of them, but that's they way they used them then. Then he had four trumpets, four trombones. He had eight saxophones, and he was playing theatres and he was playing 1812…

124.t: Dorothy Dandridge and the "Pillar to Post" soundtrack
124.s: Dandridge sang once with Armstrong in the film, whose trick arrangements had to be simplified in the recording studio.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: It was a big cabaret scene. I think I remember telling you about when we went there, Falstein (inaudible), that's the first time I met him -- Warner Brothers.

76.t: Zutty's film credits: Stormy Weather, New Orleans and others
76.s: Dance and the Singletons recall his movies, including Stormy Weather, New Orleans, Turned Up Toes, a film with Cesar Romero and Paul Douglas, and A Song Is Born with Danny Kaye.
76.q: No I don't. 'Turned Up Toes' Galliard Another picture I made was the one with the Slim Gaylord Vallee trio with Rudy Vallee and Pat O'Brian was in that picture.

238.t: Her Universal short with Ina Ray Hutton
238.s: She made a short film with Ina Ray Hutton's all-girl band, singing Real Gone Guy, around 1953-54.
238.ch: This Is Your Life and film work
238.q: Oh, I did a short with Ina Ray Hutton, Ina Ray Hutton and her Girl -- I think it was called, "No Men Allowed," or something like that, because she had all girls, you know, an all girl orchestra. And she was a charming person, I thought. She sort of faded out of the picture. I don't know what…

125.t: Hawkins band at Billy Berg's and the film Crimson Canary
125.s: The inventive band with Howard McGhee played Billy Berg's and appeared in a film, The Crimson Canary, where music was pre-recorded.
125.ch: New York with Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins
125.q: But the main thing I wanted to speak about about this group was that it was a very musical group and it was very inventive. Everybody in the band was a writer, you know. Denzil Best wrote music.
